The operator reports OperatorOutcome::NotInspected, the transaction sets TX.inspection_incomplete=1 and Transaction::inspection_incomplete() returns true, and WafConfig::detector_inspection_action defaults to RecordOnly (a miss with the signal); FailClosed interrupts the transaction instead (F02).

The libperfusion public wrapper does not scan inputs over 65536 bytes. The operator reports OperatorOutcome::NotInspected, the transaction sets TX.inspection_incomplete=1 and Transaction::inspection_incomplete() returns true, and WafConfig::detector_inspection_action defaults to RecordOnly (a miss with the signal); FailClosed interrupts the transaction instead (F02).
Unconditional-match stub, as in Go.
Registered only with the inspect-file crate feature, which host-operators also enables; the default build rejects the name.

On Unix both streams share one socket, so the combined output keeps the program's write order like Go's CombinedOutput. Non-Unix platforms use separate pipes and read stdout before stderr, which differs only when both carry output, and an over-cap verdict there can be decided from stderr, where Go reads the combined first byte.

The program runs directly, without a shell, and the 10 s deadline bounds the program and its exit wait: a killed program is reaped within a short grace, while one stuck in uninterruptible sleep is left to be reaped when the process exits rather than parking the caller.

Retained output is capped at 1 MiB. An over-cap run keeps the collected prefix and applies Go's first-byte verdict to it, then abandons the run, so a huge output still matches or misses by its first byte. Its exit status is not consulted, so a program that writes more than the cap and then exits non-zero still matches here, where Go reads the whole output and returns false on the failing status. A spawn failure, a read error, or a missed deadline reports OperatorOutcome::NotMatched, as Go returns false for every error, so a negated !@inspectFile matches on failure; a non-zero exit status stays a non-match for a run that stays within the cap, as in Go.
At most 64 runs execute at once in a process; a run above that cap reports NotMatched instead of queueing.

On Unix an abandoned reader is stopped and joined before the call returns. On other platforms a read on a pipe cannot be interrupted, so a reader a surviving descendant keeps blocked is detached and holds one descriptor and at most the cap until the last write end closes.
An empty or whitespace-only program is rejected when the rule loads, where Go accepts it and fails on every value.
The value is passed as raw bytes on Unix and converted lossily elsewhere, because other platforms have no byte path form.
Registered only with the rbl crate feature, which host-operators also enables; the default build rejects the name.

Only A/AAAA records are queried. Go also reads the TXT record, sets TX.httpbl_msg from its first entry, copies it into capture 0, and reports no match when the TXT lookup fails; without a DNS dependency this port matches on the address record alone.

A resolver failure is a plain miss, as in Go, where LookupHost returns an error and the rule does not match. A lookup past the 500 ms budget, above the 64-in-flight cap, or a failed thread spawn is also a plain miss (OperatorOutcome::NotMatched), because Go returns false on its timeout and the rule negates that result; a negated !@rbl therefore matches on failure. No host-operator outcome sets TX.inspection_incomplete or triggers FailClosed.

The configured service is trimmed of surrounding whitespace and must not be empty, so an empty service is rejected when the rule loads; Go appends it verbatim and relies on the TXT lookup to reject the self-resolving name it would build.
The value is decoded with String::from_utf8_lossy before it is appended, where Go appends the raw bytes of its value string, so invalid UTF-8 reaches the resolver as U+FFFD here.
Go regexp and byte-regexp profiles have no exact Rust equivalent; syntax, Unicode folding and malformed-byte captures need shared fixtures.
Registered only with the validate-schema crate feature; the default build rejects the name.

The schema path must be relative, contain no .. component, name a .json file, and canonicalise under the configured base directory. Type and size are read from the opened descriptor, and on Linux the descriptor's own path is confined again, which catches a symlink swapped in before the open; a descriptor path that cannot be canonicalised, such as when /proc is unavailable, is refused. On other platforms the check and the open are two steps, so the schema directory must be writable only by the process' own configuration source. Go reads the path through whatever root filesystem the embedder passed.
A schema file larger than 1 MiB is rejected before it is read, and a non-regular file is rejected.
A schema that fails to compile reports that step without quoting the schema, so a rejected schema cannot echo its contents into a log.

Every schema is compiled as 2020-12, as Go's pinned kaptinlin/jsonschema compiler does: it parses $schema but never consults it. An unknown $schema still loads, and a draft-07-only keyword shape such as tuple items or a boolean exclusiveMinimum is a compile error. format is not asserted in either engine: Go's compiler keeps AssertFormat off (compiler.go:65) and 2020-12 makes format an annotation, so a format: email schema accepts not-an-email whatever $schema declares. This changes the pre-batch behavior for a schema that declares draft-04/6/7, whose formats this port used to assert because $schema selected the draft; the pin toward Go parity made it an annotation.

The engine is this crate's jsonschema, not Go's kaptinlin/jsonschema. External $ref targets are disabled, so a reference to another document fails at compile time instead of reading an arbitrary path or URL.
A pattern matcher that cannot complete, such as one that trips the regex engine's backtrack or size limit, counts as a violation, so a pathological pattern fails closed.
Each operator compiles its own schema; Go's memoizer shares one compilation per schema content.

REQUEST_XML:/* selects all text segments stored under the literal /* key, exactly as XML:/* does, where Go's regex path drops the trailing byte of a selector with no closing slash, so REQUEST_XML:/* compiles as an empty regex and selects every XML entry, attribute values included (ledger request-xml-root-selector). Every XML/JSON selector Go's regex path leaves empty collapses the same way, such as /*, /x and //. The parser folds the variable name case before that path guard, so xml:/* and request_xml:/* also select the text segments only, while Go's rule parser enters its path branch only for the exact spellings XML and JSON (internal/seclang/rule_parser.go:124) and sends a lower-case spelling down its regex path (ledger xml-lowercase-selector). The XML processor evaluates no XPath: it flattens attribute values under //@* and all text segments under /* (coraza/src/transaction/request_body.rs:185-192). The same folded guard admits lower-case json: selectors, where Go's exact check does not.
